questions.stem: Linda Faulker, 69, is improving in ED with presumed norovirus gastroenteritis, caught after changing her 3-year-old grandson's diarrhoeal nappies. Before discharge she asks when it is safe to prepare food for others and look after the grandchildren again. What is the best advice to give her?
options: Once she has had 24 hours without any diarrhoea or vomiting and is eating normally
Once a stool PCR confirms that norovirus is no longer present
Once 48 hours have passed since her last diarrhoea or vomiting
Once a full 7 days have passed since her symptoms first began
questions.why: Norovirus is still shed and spreads easily after symptoms settle, so Australian exclusion advice (food handling, caring for children) is 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting. Pair this with soap-and-water hand washing, because alcohol rub works poorly against norovirus.
notes: 24 hours is too short for norovirus; she can still pass it on, and the standard exclusion period is 48 hours after symptoms stop.
Clearance stool testing is not used for norovirus, as PCR can stay positive for weeks; return is based on time since symptoms stopped.
A fixed 7 days from onset has no basis; exclusion is counted from when symptoms stop, and 48 hours is enough.

questions.stem: Linda, 69, with gastroenteritis, had lying BP 96/58 and HR 124 (usual BP 140/80). After a first 500 mL crystalloid bolus she is lying flat with HR 128, BP 94/54, CRT 3 s and little urine. VBG shows a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, K 3.3, lactate 1.6. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give a further 500 mL Hartmann's bolus, then reassess HR, BP and urine output
Start maintenance fluid with 20 mmol KCl at 80 mL/h and review in 4 hours
Give 1 L of 4% albumin over 30 minutes, then recheck lactate, HR, BP and urine output
Start a peripheral noradrenaline infusion aiming for a MAP of 65 mmHg
questions.why: Values still in the yellow zone after one bolus mean she is still hypovolaemic and needs more crystalloid boluses, each followed by reassessment. A balanced fluid such as Hartmann's avoids making her hyperchloraemic acidosis worse.
notes: Maintenance rates will not correct the deficit in a patient who is still hypovolaemic, and potassium should go in once she is passing urine and resuscitated.
Albumin has no advantage over crystalloid for resuscitating fluid lost to gastroenteritis, and it costs more.
Vasopressors are for hypotension that persists after adequate fluid; she has had only 500 mL despite ongoing large losses.

questions.stem: Linda, 69, takes captopril 50 mg twice daily and has been taking ibuprofen. After 8 hours of vomiting and diarrhoea her creatinine is 128 µmol/L (baseline 70) and her urea is disproportionately raised. By what mechanism does captopril lower her GFR when she is hypovolaemic?
options: Loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar vasodilation
Loss of angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction
Direct toxicity to proximal tubular cells causing tubular necrosis
Bradykinin build-up causing afferent arteriolar constriction
questions.why: When renal perfusion falls, angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole to keep glomerular pressure up. An ACE inhibitor removes this, so GFR falls. NSAIDs block afferent prostaglandin vasodilation, which is why the two together with dehydration cause prerenal AKI.
notes: This is how ibuprofen contributes, by blocking afferent prostaglandin vasodilation, not how captopril does.
ACE inhibitors cause a haemodynamic (prerenal) fall in GFR, not direct tubular toxicity; a raised urea:creatinine ratio fits a prerenal cause.
Bradykinin is a vasodilator; its build-up with ACE inhibitors causes cough and angioedema, not afferent constriction.

questions.stem: Linda, 69, is a hypertensive, diabetic ex-smoker who woke with sudden diffuse abdominal pain. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm, but the registrar wants mesenteric ischaemia kept in mind. If an embolus, for example from AF, caused it, which artery would it most likely lodge in, and why?
options: Coeliac trunk, as it is the first and shortest anterior branch of the abdominal aorta
Inferior mesenteric artery, as its narrow lumen readily traps emboli
Marginal artery at the splenic flexure, as it is a watershed end vessel
Superior mesenteric artery, as it leaves the aorta at an acute, oblique angle
questions.why: The SMA arises from the aorta at about L1, at a narrow angle and almost in line with aortic flow, so emboli pass into it easily. They usually lodge a few centimetres beyond its origin, near the middle colic branch, causing small bowel ischaemia.
notes: The coeliac trunk is short and has a rich collateral supply; it is rarely the site of embolic occlusion.
The IMA's small calibre and sharp take-off actually make embolism there uncommon, and IMA territory has good collaterals.
Watershed areas such as the splenic flexure are typical of low-flow (non-occlusive) ischaemia, not embolic occlusion.
